analysis.one_liner: Expires most new federal regulations after three years unless Congress votes to keep each one.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with zero cosponsors in July 2019, it sat in two House committees until Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have put a three-year expiration date on nearly every new rule issued by federal agencies — workplace safety standards, pollution limits, financial protections, and the like — unless Congress passed a separate law to reauthorize each one. Rules issued through formal hearings, military and foreign affairs rules, criminal enforcement rules, internal agency rules, and emergency rules were exempt. Agencies would have had to ask Congress a year in advance to keep any rule alive. The bill never moved past its referral to committees.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, regulated industries would have been the main beneficiaries: any new rule constraining a company would vanish after three years unless Congress acted, and with hundreds of rules issued each year, many would simply lapse. Companies facing new pollution limits, safety requirements, or consumer protections would get an automatic escape hatch every three years.

how_it_helps.text: Any new rule issued by a federal agency after enactment would automatically lose force three years after taking effect unless Congress specifically reauthorized it by law.
Once a rule sunset, the agency could not reissue, enforce, revise, or take any other regulatory action related to it, so lapsed rules could not be revived without new congressional action.

The bill's stated rationale, reflected in its title, is that lawmaking power belongs to Congress under Article I of the Constitution, and that requiring votes on each rule makes unelected agencies accountable to elected lawmakers.
Agencies wanting a rule kept alive would have to submit a public report justifying reauthorization a full year before the rule was set to expire, bundled with other requests.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal rules would bear the cost. Protections covering air and water pollution, workplace safety, food and drug safety, consumer finance, and more would need a fresh act of Congress every three years to survive, and with Congress's crowded calendar and thin majorities, many would lapse — leaving the public exposed to whatever practices the lapsed rules had limited.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public protected by federal rules

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection: the mechanism creates a silent way to kill regulations. Because Congress would have to affirmatively reauthorize every covered rule, any rule a majority quietly declines to schedule a vote on would expire on its own — letting protections die without anyone ever voting to kill them.

An honest supporter would have to acknowledge the workload problem: agencies issue hundreds of rules a year, and reauthorizing them one by one would swamp the congressional calendar, so many worthwhile rules would lapse for lack of attention rather than on the merits.

The bill carves out several categories — formal rulemakings, military and foreign affairs rules, criminal enforcement, agency management, and emergencies — so the exemption list itself would become a battleground over which rules deserve to survive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill advances a real constitutional principle — that Congress, not agencies, should make binding law — but the mechanism it proposes would put a three-year fuse on nearly every new federal protection and give Congress a built-in excuse to let unwanted rules die without a vote. For ordinary people, the expected cost in lapsed safety, health, and consumer protections would far outweigh the accountability benefit, especially since Congress has never demonstrated the capacity to reauthorize rules at anything close to this volume.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, where it sat with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Posey introduced the bill in the House on July 2, 2019.
The same day, it was referred to the Committee on Oversight and Reform and the Committee on the Judiciary, splitting jurisdiction between them.
On July 30, 2019, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law — the last action the bill ever received.
No other member cosponsored the bill during the Congress.
The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without either committee taking it up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people came out ahead, in the sense that the rules that protect them — on pollution, safety, and consumer finances — were never placed under a three-year expiration requirement. Businesses that would have gained an automatic escape hatch from new regulations did not get one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept its regulatory protections

for.name: Rep. Bill Posey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Oversight and Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out or scheduled action on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and its Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Took a referral of the bill, sent it to a subcommittee on July 30, 2019, and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of potential support or opposition never had a chance to appear on the record.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses generally (polluters, manufacturers, financial firms, and other companies subject to new federal rules)
industries.note: The bill would have erased any new binding rule after three years unless Congress reauthorized it, giving every regulated company an automatic deadline-based escape from new obligations. The public cost is that safety, health, and environmental protections would lapse when Congress failed to act.

Agencies would lose the power to keep their own rules in force, and could not reissue or even revise a sunsetted rule. The bill also added reporting duties, so the loss of authority came with new paperwork obligations.
